## Linear regression is the yardstick

Linear regression is the simplest model for a quantity, and the yardstick for every
method in this section: each is scored on the same new sites, and a more complex method
earns its place only by beating it. One small change, a squared input, lets the
straight line bend and find the temperature a species prefers. What neither the line
nor the curve can learn is that a count stops at zero.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## A squared input bends the line into a curve

A linear regression adds a starting value to a fixed amount for each input, the
input's coefficient times its value
([Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#linear-regression-gives-one-slope-per-input)).
One extra unit of an input changes the prediction by the same amount wherever you
start, so the prediction is a straight line in each input. A straight line cannot rise
and then fall. Adding the square of an input as one more column lets it:

$$\hat{y} = a + b x + c x^2$$

This is **polynomial regression**, and it is still linear regression. The prediction
is still a starting value plus a coefficient times each column; one of the columns
happens to be a square. "Linear" refers to how the coefficients combine, not to the
shape of the curve.

When $c$ is negative the curve has one peak, at $x = -b / 2c$. That is the shape of an
optimum: a species that does best at one temperature or depth and less well on either
side.

::: {.diagram}
![A straight line has one slope. Adding a squared input bends it into a curve with one peak, still fitted by linear regression. Beyond the data, the curve keeps going, even below zero.](img/line-to-curve.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Straight line: a plus b times the input; each extra unit of the input adds the same amount, wherever you start. Curve: a plus b times the input plus c times the input squared; the curve rises to a peak, marked optimum, and falls again; it is still linear regression, a weighted sum of columns, one of them a square. Beyond the data: a shaded band marks the range of the data, the curve peaks inside it and, dashed, keeps falling outside it on both sides, below a line marking zero. A note says a curve can follow a peak that a straight line misses, but only inside the range of the data."}
:::

Outside the range of the data, a curve keeps rising or falling, and nothing in the
model checks where it goes;
[Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd)
deals with predicting there.

## Worked example

The outcome is the survey's count of one species, with depth, temperature,
chlorophyll, salinity, seabed type and season as inputs. A quarter of the sites are
held back as test sites, as [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd)
recommends, so the models are scored on sites they have never seen. The two recipes
differ in one step: `step_poly()` adds the squares of depth and temperature, and
`raw = TRUE` keeps them as plain squares, so the coefficients mean what they do in the
equation above.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season

line_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand")

curve_recipe <- line_recipe |>
  step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE))
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()

numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
predictors = numeric + categorical

grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"]))
train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows]

# The dropped level of each column is its baseline: sand, and spring as in R.
dummies = OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False)

line_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
    ("categorical", dummies, categorical),
])

# One PolynomialFeatures per column, as step_poly() does: given both columns
# at once, it would also add depth times temperature.
def squared(column):
    return (column, Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)),
    ]), [column])

curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    squared("depth_m"),
    squared("temperature_c"),
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
     ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]),
    ("categorical", dummies, categorical),
])
```

:::

### The curve finds a peak the line misses

Both models are fitted on the training sites. The table shows the coefficients for
depth and temperature; in R, `_poly_1` is the input and `_poly_2` its square.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fit
line_fit  <- workflow(line_recipe,  linear_reg()) |> fit(train)
curve_fit <- workflow(curve_recipe, linear_reg()) |> fit(train)

bind_rows(
  tidy(line_fit)  |> mutate(model = "Linear regression"),
  tidy(curve_fit) |> mutate(model = "Polynomial regression")
) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "depth|temperature")) |>
  transmute(model, term, estimate = as.character(signif(estimate, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

def fit(recipe):
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", LinearRegression())]).fit(
        train[predictors], train["abundance"])

def coefficients(fitted, label):
    table = pd.DataFrame({"model": label,
                          "term": fitted[:-1].get_feature_names_out(),
                          "estimate": fitted[-1].coef_})
    table = table[table["term"].str.contains("depth|temperature")]
    return table.assign(estimate=table["estimate"].map(lambda v: float(f"{v:.3g}")))

line_fit = fit(line_recipe)
curve_fit = fit(curve_recipe)

pd.concat([coefficients(line_fit, "Linear regression"),
           coefficients(curve_fit, "Polynomial regression")], ignore_index=True)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: fit-numbers
#| include: false
line_coef  <- tidy(line_fit)  |> select(term, estimate) |> deframe()
curve_coef <- tidy(curve_fit) |> select(term, estimate) |> deframe()
temp_b <- curve_coef[["temperature_c_poly_1"]]
temp_c <- curve_coef[["temperature_c_poly_2"]]
optimum <- -temp_b / (2 * temp_c)
temp_range <- range(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The straight line gives temperature one coefficient,
`r num(signif(line_coef[["temperature_c"]], 2))`: each extra degree lowers the predicted
count by `r abs(signif(line_coef[["temperature_c"]], 2))` animals, in the coldest water
and the warmest alike. For the curve, $b$ is `r num(signif(temp_b, 3))` and $c$ is
`r num(signif(temp_c, 3))`. $c$ is negative, so the
curve has a peak, at $-b / 2c$ = `r round(optimum, 1)` °C, well inside the survey's
`r round(temp_range[1], 1)` to `r round(temp_range[2], 1)` °C.

Fitted through a hump, a straight line averages the rising side with the falling side,
and its one slope describes neither:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-shapes
#| fig-cap: "The predicted count across the survey's temperatures, with the other inputs held at their typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The ticks along the bottom are the training stations. Linear regression falls steadily; polynomial regression finds the peak and falls below zero in warm water."
#| fig-alt: "Two lines of predicted count against temperature, with a horizontal line marking zero and ticks along the bottom showing the temperatures of the training stations. The linear regression line declines slowly. The polynomial regression curve rises from the cold end to a peak in the middle of the range, then falls steeply and crosses zero before the warm end of the data."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
grid <- tibble(
  temperature_c     = seq(temp_range[1], temp_range[2], length.out = 200),
  depth_m           = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE),
  chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE),
  salinity_psu      = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE),
  substrate         = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)),
  season            = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season))
)

curves <- bind_rows(
  augment(line_fit, grid)  |> mutate(model = "Linear regression"),
  augment(curve_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Polynomial regression")
)

ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, .pred, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_rug(data = train, aes(temperature_c), inherit.aes = FALSE,
           sides = "b", alpha = 0.3, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Linear regression" = ml_palette[["blue"]],
                                 "Polynomial regression" = ml_palette[["orange"]]),
                      breaks = c("Linear regression", "Polynomial regression")) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count", colour = NULL,
       title = "Polynomial regression finds a peak the straight line misses")
```

:::

### The curve scores better, and predicts fewer than zero animals

Both models are scored on the test sites with the
[RMSE](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#the-test-error-is-a-typical-miss),
the typical miss in animals, and
[$R^2$](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd#one-linear-regression-shows-each-kind),
the share of the variation in the test counts that the predictions follow. The last
two columns give the lowest prediction and the number of predictions below zero.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: compare
score <- function(fitted, label) {
  predictions <- augment(fitted, test)
  tibble(
    model      = label,
    rmse       = rmse_vec(predictions$abundance, predictions$.pred),
    rsq        = rsq_trad_vec(predictions$abundance, predictions$.pred),
    lowest     = min(predictions$.pred),
    below_zero = sum(predictions$.pred < 0)
  )
}

scores <- bind_rows(
  score(line_fit,  "Linear regression"),
  score(curve_fit, "Polynomial regression")
)
scores |> mutate(across(rmse:lowest, \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error

def score(fitted, label):
    predicted = fitted.predict(test[predictors])
    truth = test["abundance"]
    return {
        "model": label,
        "rmse": round(root_mean_squared_error(truth, predicted), 2),
        "rsq": round(r2_score(truth, predicted), 2),
        "lowest": round(predicted.min(), 2),
        "below_zero": int((predicted < 0).sum()),
    }

pd.DataFrame([score(line_fit, "Linear regression"),
              score(curve_fit, "Polynomial regression")])
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: compare-numbers
#| include: false
line_score  <- scores |> filter(model == "Linear regression")
curve_score <- scores |> filter(model == "Polynomial regression")
```

On sites the models have never seen, the curve does better: $R^2$ rises from
`r round(line_score$rsq, 2)` to `r round(curve_score$rsq, 2)`, and the RMSE falls from
`r round(line_score$rmse, 2)` to `r round(curve_score$rmse, 2)` animals.

The better model is also the more impossible one. The curve predicts a negative count
at `r curve_score$below_zero` of the `r nrow(test)` test stations, the lowest
`r num(round(curve_score$lowest, 1))` animals; the line does so at `r line_score$below_zero`.
Nothing in linear regression knows that a count stops at zero, and the curve falls
steeply after its peak, so it crosses zero sooner. Setting the negative predictions to
zero hides the symptom, not the cause. [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd)
uses a model whose predictions cannot go below zero.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- Linear regression is the yardstick: every method in this section is scored against
  it on the same new sites.
- Adding a squared input bends the line into a curve with one peak. It is still linear
  regression, and it suits a species with a preferred temperature or depth.
- On the survey, the line gives temperature one slope,
  `r num(signif(line_coef[["temperature_c"]], 2))` animals per degree, while the curve finds
  a peak at `r round(optimum, 1)` °C and scores better on new sites.
- Neither knows that a count stops at zero: the curve predicts a negative count at
  `r curve_score$below_zero` of `r nrow(test)` test stations.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Change `degree = 2` to `degree = 3` in `curve_recipe`. Does the test RMSE improve,
   and what happens to the temperature curve at the cold and warm ends?
2. Draw the grid from 0 to 25 °C instead of the survey's range, and redraw the figure.
   Where does each model go outside the data?
